Pros:

* Control over which libraries / features are enabled for pretty much every single package. USE flags can be used per package, or system-wide
* extremely easy to add a patch or to edit a package. Many times as simple as putting the raw patch into a specific directory.
* extremely easy to install a newer version of a package, or hold a version back.
* package format is straightforward for writing custom packages

Cons:

* Compile time. Especially web browsers that can update frequently
* If you don't know what you're doing with USE flags, it's easy to disable things you actually need
* Dependency problems are harder to solve. With traditional package managers, you just need to wait for an update, or submit a bug report. With this distribution, sometimes the user causes the conflict with use flags or package masks. You have to resolve these yourself. Obviously there are forums and IRC for help, but it's not something you can just wait on a maintainer to fix (generally.)

So really I'd only suggest this distribution for the tweak addicts, who know their system and want complete control. I'd never recommend it to a beginner. But it is a great and fun distro for me.

Here's an ELI5:


CPUCores: Your CPU has many mini-cpus in them called cores. All apps on your computer share these, and the operating system generally tries to share work among them. With CPUCores, you're kind of reserving some of them. Saying, "My game will run on these cores, and nothing else is allowed to." In theory it's supposed to make sure your game isn't delayed by other apps. In reality, it makes barely any difference, because the operating system is already good enough at deciding how much cpu power an app needs, and giving it automatically.

Clearmem: Imagine you have a whiteboard that everyone in your office is sharing. You want to use it too, but it's full. So you take a photo, and send it to everyone in the office, then erase anything from the board that doesn't look important. Some of the coworkers actually needed what was on the board and will immediately write it back on there. Others will now be slowed down because they have to look at their phones for the whiteboard instead of just looking up from their desks. This is what clearmem does to your system memory. It just wipes away what it doesn't think is important without asking permission from the apps using it. So it can cause other apps to have problems as well. The much better choice is to tell the supervisor (the operating system) that you need some space, and it will tell everyone to write down what isn't important, and then erase it from the board so you can have the space. It is technically slower, but still more than fast enough, and as the added bonus of not causing any more problems.

>In multi-distro setup, how do you handle boot loader? Just use the boot loader of last installed Linux or is there a way to customize and use other distros boot loader?

I use rEFInd as my main boot loader, and let each distro install it's own GRUB on the EFI partition. rEFInd picks them up automatically. Don't let a distro create a separate partition for /boot, and most of them work without any modification.

> Anything else that you can suggest or caution me about.

I'd suggest not using the same home directory for all distros. You'll run into problems with different versions of software, or assumptions about where other things should be. I have a shared partition, where I put things like documents, downloads, ssh keys, etc. Then I just symlink what I need into each distro's home directory.

It's possible to set it up to boot without a second boot loader manually, assuming the kernel used by the distribution is configured with EFI stub support.

But I find it's better not to fight with the defaults. If you chain boot loaders, then you don't have to do anything manually. The distribution is free to update grub and update kernel packages, and edit all the config files it expects to be there. The alternative would possibly mean having to manually edit the rEFInd config every time a kernel is updated in some distributions. Also by bypassing GRUB this way, you MUST manually configure each kernel as well if you're using any kernel parameters at all, since they can't be auto-detected. And if you use a distribution that doesn't delete old kernels, you could end up with a menu entry in refind for every single version of the kernel installed.

Suffice to say, it's much less hassle to let the distributions assume that they have full control over the bootloader. Just think of rEFInd as a bootloader selector instead of a bootloader itself.
